title: Why We Teach
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Through the story of his first-year student Caleb in Baltimore, Stuart reflects on the right motivation for teaching. He recounts how a parent's suggestion turned into a three-year mentoring program of weekly restaurant trips, and how he came to believe his investment in Caleb had failed when the boy's life grew harder. He then confronts the 'me-centered heart': teachers want students to flourish partly to validate themselves, and because long-term flourishing is so hard to measure, they chase external affirmation, which becomes an addiction. He describes writing 'FLEE RECOGNITION' in his notebook and later facing a year of awards and recognition, then receiving a call the same day from a grown Caleb saying Stuart had made a major impact. He concludes that teachers cannot teach for awards or for grateful phone calls, only for the student himself and his long-term flourishing, and that teaching is noble work that also shapes the teacher's character.
points: Stuart argues that teachers' desire to make an impact hides a 'me-centered' need for validation that can turn into an addiction to affirmation.
Because long-term flourishing is hard to measure, teachers substitute external recognition for real evidence of impact, with corrosive effects on their relationships with colleagues.
The Caleb story shows that a teacher's sense of failure in the moment is unreliable, because planted seeds can bear fruit years later.
He concludes that neither awards nor grateful former students can fuel a career; only the student's long-term flourishing can.
He frames teaching as character-forming work for the teacher, part of 'teaching's pay' if the teacher allows it.
quotes: But by then, I was learning that results aren't guaranteed. It's just the work and the praying and the seeing how things come out. Part of the work was getting better and better at teaching, for the sake of students.

On the one hand, you do genuinely want to help your students flourish, both now and for the long term, for their sake; at the same time, you unconsciously want to help them for your sake. Nobody teaches you this.

Affirmation becomes an addiction. We start pulling jerk moves to get it. We become Those Teachers who listen autobiographically, deflating your excitement over something that your students did by quickly sharing something cool that our students did.
Yet the road to character is long. You don't arrive at Conquest of Inner Selfishness and Moratorium on Mixed Motivations in a year or two.

Affirmation, in whatever form, can't provide the fuel it takes to power a teaching career that ripples. All we can teach for is Caleb himself, both Caleb the Sixth Grader and Caleb the Adult, the latter of whom we hope we've helped equip for the climb of his Everest when he eventually defines it.
We resist the urge to compare our selves to other teachers even as we compare our data because we know this is a job of abundance, despite policies built on notions of scarcity.
We do all these things because this, teaching, is our good and noble work. We do it because from our first lesson to our last, we're a part of something bigger than us or our time.
